211   energy cover crops more closely resembles that of cover crops transformed into livestock feed, which 212   are also known as “double crops.” Due to the short growing period, energy cover crops are harvested 213   before they reach maturity. Because methanogenic potential varies little among crop species during 214   vegetative stage, the amount of biomass harvested is the key factor determining levels of biogas 215   production (Graß et al. 2013; Marsac et al. 2019). Aboveground biomass production is higher for species 216   with high growth levels, such as sorghum [Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench], corn [Zea mays L.], and 217   sunflower [Helianthus annuus L.] in the summer and triticale [x Triticosecale rimpaui Wittm.], rye 218   [Secale cereale L.], barley [Hordeum vulgare L.], and oats [Avena sativa L.] in the winter. Inputs (e.g., 219   fertilizer, irrigation water, pesticides) can be provided to further boost biomass accumulation. During 220   the summer fallow period, solar radiation levels are high, but seeding conditions can be challenging, 221   particularly in the dry regions of southern Europe, which may face water scarcity during this time of 222   year. Farmers should favor short-cycle species that are resistant to water stress, such as sunflower and 223   sorghum, and recognize that irrigation must sometimes be employed to ensure cover crop emergence 224   and biomass production. During the winter fallow period, biomass production mostly takes place in 225   spring. Farmers should thus target species with explosive growth during the early spring, such as grasses. 226   Because energy cover crops are good at accumulating biomass, they take up large amounts of nitrogen 227   from the soil and require a moderate supply of fertilizer (40–80 kg N/ha), mainly in the form of digestate; 228   using this approach can ensure sufficient yields without impairing the growth of the following crop 229   (Szerencsits 2014; Marsac et al. 2019). [SOURCE: Page_277]

230   Much research has been dedicated to management strategies for maximizing biomass production by 231   energy cover crops (Heggenstaller et al. 2008; Graß et al. 2013; Molinuevo-Salces et al. 2013, 2014; 232   Negri et al. 2014; Szerencsits 2014; Igos et al. 2016; Marsac et al. 2019; Wannasek et al. 2019). Best 233   practices for summer energy cover crops include early seeding, the use of drought-resistant species, and 234   a sufficient supply of water at seedling emergence (Marsac et al. 2019). In the case of winter energy 235   cover crops, biomass is largely harvested from April onwards, so a good approach is to delay harvesting 236   as much as possible, without overly shortening the subsequent crop’s growing period (Szerencsits 2014; 237   Marsac et al. 2019). To produce sufficient energy cover crop biomass, attention must be paid to seeding 238   and harvesting dates, which could require farmers to redesign crop rotations. It may be enough to employ 239   early varieties of cash crops and harvest them a few days or weeks in advance, in the case of summer 240   energy cover crops; for winter energy cover crops, cash crops can be seeded with a slight delay. To 241   increase the total biomass production of energy cover crops, the crop cycle can be modified either by 242   removing winter cash crops—allowing the addition of winter energy cover crops—or by introducing 243   winter cash crops that can be harvested before July—allowing the addition of summer energy cover 244   crops. [SOURCE: Page_277]

245   With regards to environmental impacts, energy cover crops should display the same services and 246   disservices as conventional cover crops during the soil cover period. These include reducing drainage; [SOURCE: Page_277]

247   protecting groundwater quality; structuring the soil; mitigating climate change thanks to higher albedo 248   levels and enhanced carbon storage in soils (via belowground biomass); maintaining biodiversity; and 249   controlling weeds. Questions remain with respect to service intensity. Because energy cover crops are 250   harvested, they do not supply any benefits associated with aboveground biomass incorporation into the 251   soil (i.e., allelopathy, green manure effects, enhanced carbon storage via aboveground biomass). It is 252   also unclear whether the use of energy cover crops could negatively affect food production because of 253   (i) the resulting changes to crop rotations and (ii) preemptive competition for water and nitrogen between 254   crop types. [SOURCE: Page_278]

255       4. From cover crop biomass production to digestate storage [SOURCE: Page_278]

256                 a. Cover crop biomass and nutrient absorption [SOURCE: Page_278]

257   Cover crop biomass production can vary markedly depending on species, management regime, soil 258   characteristics, and climatic conditions. In the summer, it is hard to obtain dense and homogenous cover 259   if plants are seeded in dried-out soil and water is scarce, given that cover crops are rarely irrigated. In 260   the fall, the important limiting factors are the total number of growing degree days and levels of global 261   radiation. Furthermore, conventional cover crops are not usually fertilized and are destroyed early on, 262   by either frost or the farmer. In Europe, aboveground biomass rarely exceeds 5 tons of dry matter (DM) 263   per hectare (ARVALIS - Institut du végétal et al. 2011; Justes et al. 2012; Hansen et al. 2021). In general, 264   energy cover crop biomass is higher because of the longer growing season, the species chosen and the 265   use of inputs (fertilizer, irrigation water, pesticides). That said, production remains highly variable for 266   summer and winter energy cover crops (3–15 t DM/ha and 2–16 t DM/ha, respectively), depending on 267   species, variety, pedoclimatic conditions, and management regime (Szerencsits 2014; Marsac et al. 268   2019). Initial results have shown that cereal-legume mixtures where the proportion of legumes does not 269   exceed 40% did not impact the cereal yield (Marsac et al. 2019). Nitrogen levels in the aboveground 270   biomass of cover crops differ based on species: they range from 13.6 to 52 g N/kg of dry matter for 271   brassicas and grasses (Justes et al. 2009; Bareha et al. 2018; Hansen et al. 2021). They are higher for 272   legumes: between 43 and 84 g N/kg of dry matter (Bareha et al. 2018; Hansen et al. 2021). Across trials 273   conducted in France and Denmark, the total nitrogen absorbed by unfertilized cover crops ranged from 274   10 to 171 kg N/ha for legumesand 9 to 89 kg N/ha for non-legumes (ARVALIS - Institut du végétal et 275   al. 2011; Hansen et al. 2021). Other studies conducted in temperate regions have found that nitrogen 276   uptake by legumes can exceed 300 kg N/ha since the plants are not limited by levels of soil nitrogen 277   (Thorup-Kristensen et al. 2003; Tonitto et al. 2006). Brassicas also have a high nitrogen uptake capacity, 278   up to 300 kg N/ha (Constantin et al. 2015); furthermore, their nitrogen acquisition rates per growing 279   degree day are higher than those of legumes when nitrogen is not limiting (Tribouillois et al. 2015). The 280   C:N ratios of cover crops generally vary from 9 to 40 (Justes et al. 2012; Hansen et al. 2021). They are 281   lower for legumes and/or cover crops that have experienced a short growing period or conditions of high [SOURCE: Page_278]

282   nitrogen availability (Justes et al. 2012). There were ranges of values for other nutrients: 2–8.2 g/kg of 283   dry matter for phosphorus; 15–52.8 g/kg of dry matter for potassium; 0.9–4 g/kg of dry matter for 284   magnesium; and 1–9 g/kg of dry matter for sulfur (MERCI tool, French National Reference Database; 285   Chambre Régionale d’Agriculture Nouvelle-Aquitaine 2020; Hansen et al. 2021). The carbon content 286   of plant dry matter can be quite consistent (40–50%; Bertrand et al. 2019). Root:shoot ratios of carbon 287   and nitrogen may differ greatly among cover crop species. Constantin et al. (2011) found that the 288   root:shoot ratio for carbon was 20% for mustard [Sinapis alba L.] versus 72% for ryegrass [Lolium 289   multiflorum Lam.]; for nitrogen, it was 6% for mustard versus 37% for ryegrass. Bispecific mixtures, 290   especially when including legumes, tend to have intermediate values between those obtained by both 291   species in sole crop. Tribouillois et al. (2016) and Couëdel et al. (2018b) observed nitrogen uptake values 292   intermediate or equal to the best species for cereal-legume and crucifer-legume mixtures. The same 293   observation was made by Couëdel et al. (2018a) for sulfur uptake. C:N and C:S ratios are always halfway 294   between both species (Tribouillois et al. 2016; Couëdel et al. 2018b, a). A recent meta-analysis showed 295   that it was very rare for a mixture to perform better than the best of the species alone on various criteria 296   including biomass production and nitrogen uptake (Florence and McGuire 2020). [SOURCE: Page_279]

297               b. Ensiling energy cover crops [SOURCE: Page_279]

298   After being harvesting, fresh energy cover crop biomass is preserved as silage until it is anaerobically 299   digested. Feedstock quality greatly affects the success of the storage process: the feedstock should have 300   high dry matter content, high accessible carbohydrate content, and low buffering capacity (Teixeira 301   Franco et al. 2016). Farmers should aim for dry matter content of 25–30% to limit fermentation, loss of 302   matter and energy, and leachate formation (Teixeira Franco et al. 2016). However, this threshold is 303   difficult to achieve when energy cover crops have a short growing period. The harvest date can be 304   delayed to allow further declines in moisture content, but increased lodging risks may result because of 305   poor weather conditions in the spring and fall (for winter and summer energy cover crops, respectively) 306   (Marsac et al. 2019). That said, it remains unclear whether dry matter content affects biochemical 307   methane potential even if it affects fermentation during ensiling (Teixeira Franco et al. 2016). In 308   addition, silage juices could be recovered to cofeed the digester. It is known that biochemical methane 309   potential can be affected by air exposure within the silo. To avoid any potential losses, it is important to 310   use good management practices, such as rapid silo closure and high levels of biomass compaction 311   (Teixeira Franco et al. 2016). [SOURCE: Page_279]

312               c. Fate of carbon during anaerobic digestion [SOURCE: Page_279]

313   During anaerobic digestion, between 20 and 95% of the substrate’s carbon content is transformed into 314   biogas (CH$_4$ and CO$_2$), depending on substrate type (Möller and Müller 2012). The percentage is higher 315   for plants that have undergone little to no transformation: 64% or 80% for a 100% corn substrate 316   (Thomsen et al. 2013; Béghin-Tanneau et al. 2019) versus 46% for corn previously digested by animals [SOURCE: Page_279]

317   (assuming that ruminal degradation of original carbon content is 70%) (Thomsen et al. 2013). For energy 318   cover crops, the amount of carbon converted into biogas during anaerobic digestion represents 43–74% 319   of initial carbon content, compared to 36–41% in the case of livestock manure (Bareha et al. 2018). 320   These figures are maxima given that the degree of degradation depends on material residence time and 321   substrate preparation (Bareha 2018). During anaerobic digestion, microorganisms preferentially degrade 322   the labile fraction of the organic substrates—avoiding recalcitrant molecules (e.g., lignin)—and produce 323   stabilized metabolites (Coban et al. 2015; Möller 2015). Past research has found differences in the 324   degree of degradation of the different organic matter fractions in energy cover crops: it is between 17 325   and 30% for the most recalcitrant fraction (lignin); between 32 and 72% for the intermediate fraction 326   (cellulose + hemicellulose); and between 10 and 75% for the soluble fraction (Bareha et al. 2019). [SOURCE: Page_280]

327               d. Fate of nutrients during anaerobic digestion [SOURCE: Page_280]

328   During anaerobic digestion, the nitrogen in crop residues is largely conserved in the digestate (Möller 329   and Müller 2012), which contrasts with the fate of carbon. Moreover, the nitrogen can change form: 330   depending on the proportion of mineral nitrogen in the substrate, further mineralization of organic 331   nitrogen can occur (Bareha et al. 2018). In fresh crop residues with N-NH$_4$+:total nitrogen ratios of 332   around zero, an average of 57% of the organic nitrogen is mineralized during anaerobic digestion; this 333   percentage is closer to 33% if residues are transformed beforehand (e.g., via ensiling or animal 334   consumption; Bareha et al. 2018). Consequently, the digestate has a higher N-NH$_4$+ content than the 335   substrate of origin, a difference that is further accentuated for crop residue digestate versus livestock 336   manure digestate (Möller and Müller 2012). The percentage of N-NH$_4$+ varies greatly, from 4 to 82% of 337   total nitrogen, depending on the substrate (Möller and Müller 2012; Nkoa 2014; Bareha et al. 2018; 338   Guilayn 2018). Even for fresh cover crop residues, the final digestate displays marked variability: from 339   1.2 g N-NH$_4$+/kg of fresh matter for barley (31% of total nitrogen) to 6.0 g N-NH$_4$+/kg of fresh matter 340   for vetch (71% of total nitrogen) (Bareha et al. 2018). This range of values results from differences in 341   substrate organic nitrogen content and in organic nitrogen biodegradability. Other nutrients are similarly 342   retained during anaerobic digestion. Levels of phosphorus range from 0.2 to 31.5 g/kg of dry matter, 343   and levels of potassium range from 0.6 to 95 g/kg of dry matter (Möller and Müller 2012; Nkoa 2014; 344   Guilayn 2018). Although phosphates, sulfates, and micronutrients (e.g., Fe, Mg, Ca) are mineralized, 345   they are not necessarily more available to plants for several reasons: (i) they precipitate as phosphates, 346   sulfide, carbonate, and hydroxides due to increases in pH; (ii) they experience sorption in the digestate’s 347   solid phase; and (iii) they undergo complexation with other compounds in solution (Möller and Müller 348   2012). Sulfur might be an issue for anaerobic digestion because at high doses it reduces the efficiency 349   of the digestion and produces a corrosive gas, H2S (Yang et al. 2016). The production of H2S can be 350   predicted by the C:S ratio of the substrates. Peu et al. (2012) found that above a C:S of 40, the amount 351   of H2S produced is treated efficiently. However, the C:S of cover crops varies between 63 and 319 for 352   a large number of species (Peu et al. 2012; Couëdel et al. 2018a; Hansen et al. 2021), above the C:S of [SOURCE: Page_280]

11 [SOURCE: Page_280]

353   pig manure at 44-51. Consequently, the use of cover crops produces H2S but in acceptable quantities to 354   be treated efficiently by the equipment already in place on the installations. [SOURCE: Page_281]

355               e. Digestate storage [SOURCE: Page_281]

356   Fermentation continues during digestate storage, and part of the carbon in the digestate is transformed 357   into methane and carbon dioxide. Approximately 8% of the carbon in the raw digestate is transformed, 358   with figures of 15% for the liquid phases and 34% for the solid phases (Bareha et al. 2021). These 359   emissions are significant since they represent 1.43 to 10.36% of methane production for a given biogas 360   unit (Liebetrau et al. 2010). If the digestate is not covered, this biogas is lost and contributes to 361   greenhouse gas emissions (Balsari et al. 2013). Digestate degradation during the storage period also 362   results in the release of nitrous oxide and ammonia, which can be limited by covering the digestate 363   (Möller 2015; Holly et al. 2017). According to different studies, nitrogen loss ranges from 9% for 364   uncovered raw cattle manure digestate to 6% for liquid digestate (Holly et al. 2017) and to 30% of 365   nitrogen for uncovered raw pig slurry digestate (Sommer 1997). Based on these figures, a recent review 366   by Walling and Vaneeckhaute (2020) found that emissions from livestock manure digestate under 367   storage conditions ranged from less than 0.01 to 0.13 kg CO$_2$-eq/kg N per day. For the moment, we have 368   not identified any figures from the digestion of cover crops. [SOURCE: Page_281]

369       5. How the anaerobic digestion of energy cover crops affects nitrogen fluxes [SOURCE: Page_281]

370               a. Nitrogen availability for crops [SOURCE: Page_281]

371   Upon cover crop destruction, soil levels of mineral nitrogen are often 50% lower than those associated 372   with bare soil because cover crops absorb nitrogen, a phenomenon that is particularly pronounced in dry 373   climates (Tribouillois et al. 2016; Alvarez et al. 2017; Meyer 2020). The level of mineral nitrogen 374   available to the following crop is strongly correlated with cover crop termination date and winter 375   drainage intensity. Later destruction dates result in greater differences relative to what is seen on bare 376   soil because the absorption period is longer and growth is faster in the spring. Lower levels of drainage 377   have the same effect because mineral nitrogen remains in the bare soil while it is absorbed by the cover 378   crop. When levels of soil organic matter and cover crop mineralization are insufficient in the early 379   spring, the low quantities of mineral nitrogen may induce preemptive competition, resulting in nitrogen 380   stress when the next crop begins growing (Thorup-Kristensen et al. 2003; Marcillo and Miguez 2017). 381   However, cover crops may furnish nitrogen to the subsequent crop via green manure effects. Green 382   manure effects result because (i) the growing cover crop takes up mineral nitrogen that would otherwise 383   leach away during winter and (ii) mineralization releases this nitrogen after the cover crops are 384   incorporated into the soil, making it available to the next crop. The degree of these effects depends on 385   the cover crop’s nitrogen uptake efficiency; residue mineralization dynamics; and leaching risks during 386   the drainage period. When legumes are used as cover crops (by themselves or in combination with non- 387   legumes), the fixation of atmospheric nitrogen can boost green manure effects. Furthermore, the C:N [SOURCE: Page_281]

388   ratio can shape the level and timing of the nitrogen available for the following crop (Jensen et al. 2005; 389   Justes et al. 2009). Residues with a ratio of less than 13 resulted in immediate net positive nitrogen 390   mineralization; in contrast, residues with a ratio of more than 26 resulted in net nitrogen immobilization 391   over the five-month incubation period. For residues with intermediate ratios, temporary immobilization 392   occurred during the first few weeks but was then followed by net mineralization (Justes et al. 2009). It 393   is difficult to reliably determine the range of nitrogen made available to subsequent crops by cover crops 394   because of all the aforementioned factors. Justes et al. (2012) tried to establish potential orders of 395   magnitude based on the research to date. They found available nitrogen ranges of −20 to +10%, −10 to 396   +30%, and +10 to +50% of absorbed N from grasses, crucifers, and legumes, respectively. [SOURCE: Page_282]

397   When digestate is applied to fields, the nitrogen made available to crops is the sum of the mineral 398   nitrogen present in the digestate and the relative amount of organic nitrogen that mineralizes in the 399   months following application. This figure corresponds almost entirely to the amount of N-NH$_4$+, since 400   only 10–20% of the organic nitrogen is mineralized within six months (based on studies of manure 401   digestates) (Möller and Müller 2012). Since organic nitrogen is mineralized during anaerobic digestion, 402   nitrogen in energy cover crop digestate should be more readily available than nitrogen in cover crop 403   residues (Möller and Müller 2012; Bareha et al. 2018). For example, it has been found that a mean 404   energy cover crop digestate input of 30 t/ha should provide 37–179 kg N-NH$_4$+/ha (Bareha et al. 2018). 405   Moreover, digestate application could be timed to better correspond to crop demands for nitrogen. [SOURCE: Page_282]

406   Energy cover crops are particularly likely to provoke preemptive competition since they are harvested 407   late and are likely to deplete the mineral nitrogen in the soil as they grow. On the other hand, avoiding 408   the incorporation of cover crops with high C:N ratios can limit or prevent nitrogen immobilization. 409   Producing an energy cover crop yield of 4.5 t dry matter/ha requires the uptake of 60–100 kg of nitrogen, 410   which could cause nitrogen stress for the next crop. By providing a source of nitrogen, such as digestate 411   fertilizer, it may be possible to both meet the needs of cover crops and reduce the risk of nitrogen stress 412   for the subsequent cash crop (Szerencsits 2014). While the latter sometimes occurs after winter energy 413   cover crops (Szerencsits 2014; Marsac et al. 2019), it is less common after summer energy cover crops. 414   Indeed, the initial nitrogen requirements of winter cash crops are often low enough that nitrogen uptake 415   by cover crops does not have a lasting impact. For example, Szerencsits (2014) did not observe any 416   nitrogen stress after the use of a summer energy cover crop. However, in simulations comparing crop 417   cycles with and without energy cover crops, it was necessary to fertilize winter wheat at higher levels 418   when the cash crop followed an energy cover crop (+30–80 kg N/ha) to maintain yields at control levels 419   (as defined in Launay et al. 2020). Thus, the risk of nitrogen stress could be lowered by providing 420   mineral or organic fertilizer to the cash crop. Another solution could be utilizing an energy cover crop 421   mixture containing legumes (Valkama et al. 2015). [SOURCE: Page_282]

422   In conclusion, anaerobic digestion can help promote the green manure effects of energy cover crops as 423   long as the digestate contains levels of available nitrogen that can compensate for nitrogen losses during 424   storage and digestate application. At the very least, removing residues from fields can prevent the 425   nitrogen immobilization that can result from energy cover crops with high C:N ratios (Brozyna et al. 426   2013). Moreover, digestate application can be optimally timed to better respond to the nitrogen needs 427   of cash crops (Möller and Stinner 2009). [SOURCE: Page_283]

433   When nitrogen fertilizer is applied, the degree of ammonia volatilization depends on fertilizer 434   characteristics (pH, NH$_4$+ content, dry matter content), soil characteristics (pH), the application method 435   (surface vs. injection), and climatic conditions (temperature, wind speed, rainfall) (Ni et al. 2012; Möller 436   2015). Higher pH and NH$_4$+ content both enhance volatilization (Möller 2015). Temperature and wind 437   speed are positively correlated with the degree of volatilization because they promote ammonia’s 438   transition from its liquid phase to its gaseous phase; the occurrence of rainfall immediately after 439   application strongly reduces volatilization (Ni et al. 2012). Since volatilization occurs at the interface 440   with the atmosphere, injecting the fertilizer limits its exposure, reducing volatilization (Webb et al. 2010; 441   Maris et al. 2021). Similarly, low levels of dry matter content allow the fertilizer to better infiltrate the 442   soil, also reducing volatilization. Consequently, the identity of the crop in place when fertilizer 443   application occurs can have an indirect effect on volatilization by slowing down infiltration; for 444   example, the presence of corn will result in less volatilization than the presence of grasslands or wheat 445   because the soil is largely bare under corn (Ni et al. 2012; Quakernack et al. 2012). The same thing for 446   the presence of crop residues (Maris et al. 2021). Studies have found that volatilization is generally 447   higher for digestate than for slurry (Table 1, S$_1$). Increases in pH and NH$_4$+ levels during anaerobic 448   digestion should have a marked effect on volatilization. However, some work has observed a decrease 449   in volatilization for digestate versus untreated slurry when the former is more fluid than the latter 450   (Chantigny et al. 2004, 2007, 2009). Very little research has considered anaerobic digestion in areas 451   with arable crops but no livestock, which means that there have been few examinations of digestate 452   serving as a substitute for mineral fertilizer. In their meta-analysis, Pan et al. (2016) found that, on 453   average, mineral fertilizers lose 18% of applied nitrogen to volatilization, recognizing that urea releases 454   the most emissions and that substituting in non-urea-based fertilizers can reduce volatilization by 75%. 455   Chantigny et al. (2007) found that digestate emitted three times more ammonia than did mineral 456   fertilizer, while Wolf et al. (2014) and Quakernack et al. (2012) found much larger differences since 457   emissions from the mineral fertilizer control occurred at levels deemed to be negligible. On the contrary, 458   Zilio et al. (2021) found that with good spreading practices, i.e. injecting the digestate directly, no 459   difference was visible with urea. [SOURCE: Page_285]

460   Most studies to date have looked at digestates produced from monofermented slurry. Digestates resulting 461   from the codigestion of crop residues are more viscous than are pure slurry digestates (Plöchl et al., 2009 462   in Quakernack et al., 2012). Thus, infiltration-mediated reductions in volatilization are probably less 463   pronounced for crop residue digestates. The few studies examining digestates from monofermented or 464   cofermented crops have found that 6 to 29% of the N-NH$_4$+ supplied is released via volatilization (Ni et 465   al. 2012; Quakernack et al. 2012; Wolf et al. 2014), which falls within the value range for digestates of 466   all origins (6–42% of the N-NH$_4$+ or total nitrogen supplied). In the small number of studies where the 467   digestate was injected, ammonia emissions drop to 4-12% of the N-NH$_4$+ supplied (Wulf et al. 2002; 468   Zilio et al. 2021; Maris et al. 2021). In addition, it is important to recognize that the use of nitrogen [SOURCE: Page_285]

477   Nitrate leaching occurs during the drainage period. The best way to minimize leaching is to keep soil 478   mineral nitrogen as low as possible before and during this time. One way to achieve this outcome is by 479   planting a fall cover crop, which will take up mineral nitrogen from the soil. On bare soils, such an 480   approach efficiently limits nitrate leaching, mainly by reducing soil mineral nitrogen but also by 481   decreasing drainage (Justes et al. 2012; Tribouillois et al. 2016; Meyer et al. 2019). The degree of 482   efficacy is species dependent: on average, non-legumes versus legumes reduce leaching by 70% and 483   40%, respectively (Tonitto et al. 2006; Tribouillois et al. 2016). [SOURCE: Page_288]

484   Fertilizer use may increase leaching risks if application takes place in the fall just before the drainage 485   period and/or if too much is employed. The European Union's Nitrate Directive (91/676/EEC) prohibits 486   applying mineral nitrogen fertilizers, as well as some organic nitrogen fertilizers (with C:N ratios < 8), 487   including digestates, to winter crops seeded in the fall. It similarly prohibits the use of all fertilizer types 488   on bare soil from early summer to February, before spring crops are planted, if no cover crops are seeded. 489   Medium- and long-term leaching risks can also be increased by higher levels of soil organic matter, 490   which can arise from repeated cover crop use or the application of organic amendments. In such cases, 491   levels of mineralized nitrogen will climb (Constantin et al. 2011) if fertilizer quantities are not 492   concomitantly reduced (Schröder et al. 2007; Constantin et al. 2012; Girault et al. 2019). In the short 493   term, using digestate as fertilizer does not increase leaching risks if fertilizer levels are calculated based 494   on the nitrogen use efficiency for the digestate and if the digestate is applied when nitrate leaching risks 495   are low, such as after the planting of a crop with high nitrogen uptake (Matsunaka et al. 2006) (Table 2, 496   S$_2$). [SOURCE: Page_288]

497   During the winter fallow period, leaching risks can be reduced by growing energy cover crops without 498   fertilizer; the effect is similar to that obtained with cover crops. When Riau et al. (2021) tested the 499   efficacy of three energy cover crop species, they found that black oat reduced leaching more than did 500   ryegrass or forage rapeseed because the former had faster, more uniform development. When black oat 501   was grown without fertilizer as an energy cover crop and harvested in the spring, it was more effective 502   than the same species terminated early and left in the field as a cover crop (Möller and Stinner 2009; 503   Gunnarsson et al. 2011). Indeed, when residues undergo mineralization in the late fall and early spring, 504   it creates the opportunity for the nitrogen absorbed by the cover crop to leach (Tribouillois et al. 2016). 505   In contrast, the digestate created from the harvested energy cover crops is applied at a time when 506   leaching risks are lower (Möller and Stinner 2009; Gunnarsson et al. 2011). Applying fertilizer to energy 507   cover crops does not appear to diminish their ability to reduce nitrate leaching. First, Heggenstaller et 508   al. (2008) observed lower levels of leaching in systems with energy cover crops versus in systems with 509   bare soil despite the higher levels of nitrogen fertilizer usage across the crop succession. Second, 510   modeling research showed that, when identical species were used, spring-fertilized, harvested energy 511   cover crops reduced leaching more than unfertilized cover crops that were destroyed a couple of weeks 512   early (Szerencsits 2014; Malone et al. 2018). Malone et al. (2018) found that fertilized, harvested rye [SOURCE: Page_288]

513   reduced leaching by 18% compared to unfertilized, unharvested rye and by 54% compared to what was 514   seen on bare soil. Similarly, Szerencsits (2014) found that, in multiyear experiments, fertilized winter 515   energy cover crops reduced leaching by 20% compared to the same species when destroyed 15 days 516   earlier and by 25% compared to what was seen on bare soil. This result could be explained by greater 517   biomass production leading to a larger reduction in drainage (Szerencsits 2014) or the decrease in 518   nitrogen mineralization due to residue removal (Malone et al. 2018). Summer energy cover crops also 519   seem to be effective in reducing leaching during the following winter compared to what is seen on bare 520   soil in summer (Szerencsits 2014; Girault et al. 2019). [SOURCE: Page_289]

521   Clearly, cover crops have a demonstrated ability to reduce leaching. Initial studies of energy cover crops 522   suggest that they display this function, which is sometimes even enhanced. Managing energy cover 523   crops in specific ways can affect nitrate leaching dynamics: (i) leaching can be reduced by producing 524   more biomass and avoiding asynchrony between residue mineralization and nitrogen uptake by the 525   following crop, and (ii) leaching may be increased in the medium to long term if nitrogen fertilizer is 526   used. It is important to underscore that long-term research in this area remains scarce, and it is necessary 527   to further explore the effects of crop cycle management when rotations include energy cover crops. [SOURCE: Page_289]

528               d. Nitrous oxide emissions [SOURCE: Page_289]

534   Nitrous oxide (N2O) is emitted mainly during denitrification, i.e. the transformation of NO$_3$− into N$_2$, as 535   an intermediate product under anaerobic conditions. A small portion of N2O is also emitted as a co- 536   product during nitrification, i.e. the transformation of NH$_4$+ into NO$_2$− then into NO$_3$− under aerobic 537   conditions (Hénault et al. 2012). Both reactions are influenced by the availability of their substrate (NH$_4$+ 538   for nitrification and NO$_3$− for denitrification) (Hénault et al. 2012; Nicholson et al. 2017) and organic 539   carbon can boost the activity of denitrifying bacteria if it is easily mobilized/degradable (Möller and 540   Stinner 2009). Beyond that, N2O emissions are mostly influenced by climatic conditions: temperature 541   and moisture (Petersen 1999; Hénault et al. 2012). Soil moisture above a certain threshold promotes 542   denitrification by creating anoxic conditions (Möller and Stinner 2009). [SOURCE: Page_291]

543   Within crop cycles, there is no clear consensus on the effect of cover crops on N2O emissions (Blanco- 544   Canqui et al. 2015; Kaye and Quemada 2017; Abdalla et al. 2019; Guenet et al. 2020). During their 545   growth, they reduce the amount of N available to microorganisms and the amount of nitrate leached, 546   thus reducing the risk of direct and indirect N2O emissions. On the other hand, the decomposition of 547   their residues after their destruction releases N2O which tends to offset the previous effect (Viard et al. 548   2013; Blanco-Canqui et al. 2015; Guenet et al. 2020; Abalos et al. 2022). The magnitude of N2O 549   emissions depends on the C:N ratio of residues, their rate of decomposition and their incorporation or 550   not into soil (Guenet et al. 2020; Abalos et al. 2022). For example, several studies have found an overall 551   increase in N2O emissions with the insertion of legume cover crops due to their low C:N (Tribouillois 552   et al. 2018; Abdalla et al. 2019; Guenet et al. 2020). [SOURCE: Page_291]

553   Since digestates are richer in mineral nitrogen but poorer in labile carbon than their substrates of origin, 554   their use as fertilizers could have contrasting impacts on nitrous oxide emissions. No consistent pattern 555   has been seen in past research comparing the effects of digestates with their substrates of origin (Table 556   3, S$_3$). When the soil is rich in carbon, either because it is covered by grassland or because of its crop 557   history, labile carbon is no longer limiting denitrification, and digestate use is no longer advantageous 558   (Vallejo et al. 2006; Pelster et al. 2012; Corré and Conijn 2016). Under dry conditions, nitrous oxide 559   emissions largely arise from nitrification, whose rate outstrips that of denitrification. In this case, the 560   supply of NH$_4$+ determines the level of nitrous oxide emissions (Möller and Stinner 2009). Reviewing 561   available studies, we found an average field emissions factor for digestates of 0.52% (0.08–1.9%) of the 562   total nitrogen applied. This figure is lower than the reference emissions factor provided by the IPCC 563   (1%). The digestate application method influences the emissions factor. For example, injection reduces 564   volatilization and increases denitrification (Wulf et al. 2002; Thomsen et al. 2010). [SOURCE: Page_291]

565   To date, only two studies have compared the effects of using crop residue digestates to leaving cover 566   crop residues in the field; one was a field study, and the other was a modeling study (Möller and Stinner 567   2009; Szerencsits 2014). They reached the same conclusion: compared to terminating and incorporating 568   cover crops into the soil, removing energy cover crop biomass to later return it as digestate seems to [SOURCE: Page_291]

569   reduce nitrous oxide emissions. This difference can be explained by the lower levels of labile carbon in 570   the digestate versus in the incorporated cover crop (Möller and Stinner 2009). [SOURCE: Page_292]

571               e. Synthesis of the nitrogen balance [SOURCE: Page_292]

572 [SOURCE: Page_292]

573   Figure 2. Schematic representation of the nitrogen balance after the incorporation of aboveground 574   cover crop biomass into the soil (on the left) or the application of digestate obtained from 575   anaerobically digested aboveground cover crop biomass (on the right). In both scenarios, initial cover 576   crop nitrogen content is the same (100 units) and the mineralization period is short (5–6 months). 577   Each number is a percentage of the original value. The cover crops’ nitrogen mineralization figures 578   were obtained from Justes et al. (2012); the nitrogen mineralization figures associated with anaerobic 579   digestion were obtained from Bareha et al. (2018); and the digestate mineralization figures were 580   obtained from Möller and Müller (2012). In both scenarios, we consider that ammonia volatilization 581   took place during digestate storage and application. For the storage period, we considered that, on 582   average, 20% of the N-NH$_4$+ volatilized (Sommer 1997; Holly et al. 2017). For the application period, 583   we assumed the same average level of volatilization (20%), based on figures for crop residues 584   digestates (Table 1). The nitrogen balance represented here focuses on the mineralization of the 585   nitrogen in cover crop residues in the soil. It does not represent nitrous oxide emissions or nitrate 586   leaching. Norg: organic nitrogen; Nmin: mineral nitrogen. [SOURCE: Page_292]

587   To summarize, we compared the nitrogen balance of a cropping system using multiservice cover crops 588   and a cropping system using digestate produced via the anaerobic digestion of energy cover crops 589   (Figure 2). When the systems start with the same initial amount of nitrogen, the nitrogen potentially 590   available to the plants across the crop rotation depends on the amount of available nitrogen added and 591   lost (i.e., nitrogen is preserved during anaerobic digestion). Nitrogen mineralization during anaerobic 592   digestion and the transformation of green manures into a controllable fertilizer increased nitrogen 593   availability. With regards to the nitrogen lost, we saw no increase in nitrous oxide emissions, an increase 594   in volatilization after digestate creation, and a potential decrease in leaching. Overall, digestate use [SOURCE: Page_292]

597       6. How the anaerobic digestion of energy cover crops affects carbon dynamics [SOURCE: Page_293]

598   By fixing atmospheric carbon dioxide, cover crops can increase the amount of carbon stored in the soil 599   (Blanco-Canqui et al. 2015; Poeplau and Don 2015; Kaye and Quemada 2017; Tribouillois et al. 2018; 600   Jian et al. 2020). Incorporating the above- and belowground biomass of cover crops could result in the 601   storage of 320 kg C/ha per year, based on a meta-analysis by Poeplau and Don (2015), or even 560 kg 602   C/ha per year, according to a meta-analysis by Jian et al. (2020). In France, the proportion in the cover 603   crops of potential remaining carbon after application to soil is 28% on average, similar in magnitude to 604   that of grain straw (Justes et al. 2012). The main factors driving carbon storage levels are the frequency 605   of cover crop inclusion and cover crop biomass (Launay et al. 2021). Species identity also has an effect, 606   given differences in C:N ratios. The meta-analysis by Jian et al. (2020) showed that cover crop C:N 607   ratios tend to negatively correlate with the amount of carbon stored in the soil. Residues with high C:N 608   ratios are hardly stabilized due to the lower carbon use efficiency of decomposers (Sinsabaugh et al. 609   2016) arising from stoichiometric constraints in organic matter decomposition; microorganisms C:N 610   ratios vary generally between 6 and 11 (Bertrand et al. 2019). Furthermore, it is important to look at the 611   distribution of carbon in aboveground versus belowground biomass. Indeed, the belowground sources 612   of organic carbon (i.e., roots and rhizodeposition) contribute more to soil carbon levels than do 613   aboveground sources (Chenu et al. 2019). Due to their physical and chemical nature and incorporation 614   depths, belowground carbon sources are more effectively stabilized by adsorption or physical protection 615   (Chenu et al. 2019). [SOURCE: Page_293]

616   Anaerobic digestion increases substrate stability (i.e., Stumpe et al. 2012; Wentzel et al. 2015; Coban et 617   al. 2015; Möller 2015). The organic carbon remaining in digestate is at least 50% more stable than it is 618   in the initial substrate (Chen et al. 2012; Thomsen et al. 2013; Béghin-Tanneau et al. 2019). 619   Consequently, carbon sequestration is equivalent in the initial crop biomass and its various byproducts 620   (animal digested and/or biogas plant digested) and corresponds to 12–14% of the carbon present at the 621   start, according to Thomsen et al. (2013). Other work has found that the digestion of corn results in a 622   sequestration level of 23% of the carbon initially present in corn; in contrast, direct incorporation of 623   corn residues does not result in carbon sequestration but rather in the release of 4% of the initial carbon 624   (Béghin-Tanneau et al. 2019). This result primarily arises because the fresh biomass triggered a 625   significant priming effect on soil organic matter mineralization. A temporary inhibition of certain 626   microbial activities after digestate application has been observed, which contrasts with the boost in 627   response to slurry (Abubaker et al. 2015). Chen et al. (2012) had already demonstrated that digestate 628   use had less of a priming effect on soil organic matter degradation than did crop residue incorporation. [SOURCE: Page_293]

629   Marsac et al. (2019) identified some factors affecting how energy cover crops can influence carbon 630   storage. Using above- and belowground biomass data in AMG model, they observed that harvested 631   energy cover crops could result in as much carbon storage as incorporated cover crops grown over 632   shorter periods without fertilizer (and that thus produced less biomass). Indeed, energy cover crops 633   grown over longer periods with fertilizer would leave behind, post harvest, quantities of stubble (1–2 t 634   dry matter/ha depending on cutting height) and roots (~20% of total biomass) equivalent to quantities 635   of cover crop residues. Choosing a cover crop species with a high root:shoot ratio, such as grass 636   (Constantin et al. 2011), could (i) enhance carbon returns via belowground biomass and (ii) provide 637   carbon more effectively stabilized than aboveground biomass (Chenu et al. 2019). Marsac et al. (2019) 638   found that, if the resulting digestate was applied as fertilizer, the levels of stored carbon would exceed 639   those associated with incorporated cover crops. Subsequently, Szerencsits (2014) assessed the humic 640   balance using the above findings in conjunction with the method described in Kolbe (2007). It was found 641   that applying the digestate derived from the aboveground biomass more efficiently stored carbon than 642   leaving the biomass in place as residues. [SOURCE: Page_294]

643 644   Figure 3. Schematic representation of the carbon balance after the incorporation of aboveground 645   cover crop biomass into the soil (on the left) or the application of digestate obtained from 646   anaerobically digested aboveground cover crop biomass (on the right). In both scenarios, initial cover 647   crop carbon content is the same (100 units). Each number is a percentage of the original value. The 648   figures for the carbon mineralization of cover crop residues are based on the decomposition of corn 649   (i.e., serving as a summer energy cover crop) in Thomsen et al. (2013) and Béghin-Tanneau et al. 650   (2019) and on the decomposition of winter cover crops in Justes et al. (2012). The figures for the 651   cover crop decomposition via anaerobic digestion were taken from Thomsen et al. (2013), Bareha et 652   al. (2018), and Béghin-Tanneau et al. (2019). We assumed that, on average, 20% of the digestate’s 653   carbon was lost during storage (Bareha et al. 2021). The figures for the decomposition of cover crop 654   digestate were taken from Thomsen et al. (2013) and Béghin-Tanneau et al. (2019). Corg: organic 655   carbon. [SOURCE: Page_294]

656   In conclusion, our initial results suggest that the use of energy cover crops can have rather positive 657   impacts on carbon storage, when the results are compared to those for cover crops incorporated into the 658   soil (Figure 3). Although some carbon is lost during anaerobic digestion, net levels of soil organic carbon 659   are seemingly unaltered because (i) biomass production increases, increasing the amount of carbon 660   returned below ground and (ii) the remaining carbon is stabilized during anaerobic digestion. However, 661   this assessment is based on a handful of studies. Some results are still being discussed and investigated, 662   such as the extent of carbon stabilization during anaerobic digestion compared to carbon losses in biogas 663   or the amount of above-ground and root biomass left in the field by energy cover crops compared to 664   traditional cover crops. [SOURCE: Page_295]

665       7. How the anaerobic digestion of energy cover crops affects soil biological activity [SOURCE: Page_295]

666               a. Microbial activity [SOURCE: Page_295]

667   During their growth, cover crops increase microbial abundance and activity via their inputs of carbon 668   from root exudates and root turnover (Elfstrand et al. 2007; Blanco-Canqui et al. 2015; Finney et al. 669   2017). A recent meta-analysis from Muhammad et al. (2021) found that cover crops significantly 670   increase microbial biomass compared to a bare soil from 24 to 51% depending on the indicator. On 671   average, they increase the abundance of bacteria by 15% and the abundance of fungi by 19%, thus 672   increasing the fungi/bacteria ratio. In general, non-legumes increase the abundance of microorganisms 673   slightly more than legumes due to higher C substrate supply through higher biomass production. In 674   addition, bacteria and fungi respond differently to these two groups of species. Non-legumes favor fungi 675   because they are specialized in the decomposition of high C:N residues, whereas bacteria specialized in 676   low C:N residues are favored by legumes. Among fungi, arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) are 677   particularly important for crop production because they improve nutrient uptake and provide resistance 678   to drought and soil pathogens (Soti et al. 2016). In addition, they can have a stabilizing effect on the soil 679   by entangling soil particles with their mycelium or by sticking them together with glomalin, which is a 680   glycoprotein produced by AMF that acts as a glue (García-González et al. 2018). Because they live in 681   symbiosis with their host plants, fallow periods are particularly detrimental to mycorrhizal fungi (Soti 682   et al. 2016). On average, cover crops increase AMF abundance, AMF root colonization and AMF spore 683   density by 26%, 13%, and 47%. Legumes had slightly less effect than non-legumes because increased 684   N returns may be deleterious to AMF root colonization (Muhammad et al. 2021). Schipanski et al. 685   (2014) calculated that after a winter cover crop, the roots of the following crop were colonized at 100% 686   of their potential by AMF against 85% if the soil was left bare during winter. Cover crops residue 687   management has an impact on microbial community abundance and structure. Exporting residues as 688   well as leaving them on the surface reduces the abundance of bacteria (+10% relative to bare soil) 689   compared to incorporating them (+25% relative to bare soil). The abundance of fungi is not impacted, 690   in all cases it is increased. But on AMF in particular, exporting residues improves root colonization less [SOURCE: Page_295]

691   (+5%) than incorporating residues (+50%) and seems to have a little less effect than residues left on the 692   surface (+10%) (Muhammad et al. 2021). Finally, cover crops also tend to increase the size of earthworm 693   populations, resulting in increased water infiltration and soil aggregate stability (Blanco-Canqui et al. 694   2015). [SOURCE: Page_296]

695   In the short term, digestate use tends to increase soil microbial activity, compared to the use of mineral 696   fertilizers or no fertilizers, although the boost is less than that provided by undigested substrates (based 697   on measurements of induced respiration; Fuchs et al. 2008; Abubaker et al. 2015; Möller 2015; Gómez- 698   Brandón et al. 2016; Risberg et al. 2017). This climb in microbial activity is not due to the digestate 699   adding microorganisms to the soil since such microorganisms do not persist in the soil (Fuchs et al. 700   2008; Stumpe et al. 2012; Coelho et al. 2020). Nor is it correlated with the quantity of carbon supplied 701   (Abubaker et al. 2015). Instead, it is associated with the quality of carbon supplied (Stumpe et al. 2012; 702   Wentzel and Joergensen 2016). DNA analysis and the quantification of taxon-specific growth rates have 703   revealed that a shift may occur in microbial communities due to the lack of readily degradable organic 704   matter (Chen et al. 2012; Abubaker et al. 2013). Fast-growing microorganisms (r-strategists) that 705   preferentially degrade labile organic matter disappear; they are replaced by slow-growing 706   microorganisms (K-strategists) that more efficiently degrade recalcitrant organic matter. This change 707   induces a modification in the ratio of fungi to bacteria (Chen et al. 2012). Differences between treatments 708   tend to fade a few months or years into digestate use (Walsh et al. 2012b; Abubaker et al. 2013; Möller 709   2015; Gómez-Brandón et al. 2016; Sadet-Bourgeteau et al. 2018). Consequently, a single dose of 710   exogenous organic matter has a temporary effect on microbial communities, depending on dose size. In 711   the case of repeated applications, the effects on microbial communities can be long lasting and 712   associated with changes in soil chemical characteristics such as pH, cation exchange capacity, and soil 713   organic carbon (Sadet-Bourgeteau et al. 2018). Several studies have shown that soil type also has a 714   significant impact: clay soils are more resilient than sandy soils (Walsh et al. 2012b; Abubaker et al. 715   2013; Wentzel et al. 2015). If a cover crop is in place when fertilizer is applied, microbial population 716   size is not directly affected by the fertilizer’s physicochemical characteristics, but is rather indirectly 717   affected by the characteristics’ impact on plant growth (Terhoeven-Urselmans et al. 2009; Walsh et al. 718   2012b; Abubaker et al. 2013). [SOURCE: Page_296]

719               b. Earthworms [SOURCE: Page_296]

720   Rollett et al. (2020) observed a positive correlation between the amount of organic matter supplied and 721   the increase in earthworm population size. Sizmur et al. (2017) has shown that it is the quantity of energy 722   provided by the organic matter that matters most; it is therefore organic matter quality that strongly 723   affects earthworms. Digestate is a source of food for earthworms, particularly anecic earthworms. In the 724   short term, digestate use increases earthworm abundance (Clements et al. 2012) and biomass, as seen in 725   field and microcosm studies (Ernst et al. 2008; Koblenz et al. 2015; Sizmur et al. 2017). 726   earthworms are not able to directly consume organic matter from digestate (Ernst et al. 2008), but they 727   can still benefit from the input of energy by consuming the waste generated by anecic earthworms 728   (Koblenz et al. 2015). In some cases, short-term mortality has resulted from the high quantity of 729   ammonium introduced by larger doses of digestate or slurry (> 170 kg N/ha) (Johansen et al. 2015; 730   Tigini et al. 2016; Renaud et al. 2017; Rollett et al. 2020). Sizmur et al. (2017) showed that, when 731   equivalent levels of carbon were used, straw increased the biomass of an anecic earthworm, Lumbricus 732   terrestris, significantly more than did plant digestate because of the higher energy input. Similarly, in a 733   field study, Frøseth et al. (2014) observed that the immediate incorporation of green manure increased 734   the size of the earthworm population compared to the use of plant digestate. In the long term, such 735   differences seem to disappear (Johansen et al. 2015; Koblenz et al. 2015; Rollett et al. 2020). However, 736   there are no long-term studies on the impacts of directly incorporating cover crop biomass into the soil 737   versus returning later in the form of digestate. [SOURCE: Page_297]

738       8. The impact of energy cover crops and their digestate on water dynamics [SOURCE: Page_297]

739   Cover crops can have complicated effects on groundwater recharge. First, by covering the soil, they can 740   increase transpiration and reduce evaporation (Qi and Helmers 2010; Nielsen et al. 2015; Tribouillois et 741   al. 2016). Second, they can increase water infiltration and reduce runoff (Snapp et al. 2005; Blanco- 742   Canqui et al. 2015; Yu et al. 2016). A recent meta-analysis by Meyer et al. (2019) found that, in most 743   studies, cover crops decreased drainage, although the results were highly variable (−110 to +40 mm). 744   Depending on climatic conditions, this reduction in drainage may represent a small or a large percentage 745   of annual water drainage, which could have major implications for water recharge in dry regions. Cover 746   crop biomass seems to be one of the main determinant factors, with seeding date close behind (Meyer 747   et al. 2020; Tribouillois et al. (2018). Tribouillois et al. (2018) observed that increases in cover crop 748   biomass were strongly correlated with increases in evapotranspiration and decreases in drainage. 749   However, at a certain threshold of biomass (< 2.5 t dry matter/ha) or leaf area index values, 750   evapotranspiration showed no further increases (Meyer et al. 2020). Based on this work, advancing 751   seeding by one month can result in a threefold difference in the degree of drainage reduction; the 752   termination date does not affect drainage but does affect soil water levels for the next crop. Based on 753   these findings, the large quantities of biomass produced by energy cover crops should not significantly 754   reduce drainage, compared to what is seen for multiservice cover crops. However, the seeding date 755   should be chosen so as to trade off between biomass production and groundwater recharge. In any case, 756   the broader-scale use of cover crops (whether multiservice or energy) could create challenges for 757   groundwater recharge, an issue should be assessed. [SOURCE: Page_297]

758   The above increase in evapotranspiration could result in a water deficit for the following summer crop. 759   The depletion of water reserves in surface has often been seen in association with multiservice cover 760   crops or energy cover crops terminated/harvested in the spring (Krueger et al. 2011; Alonso-Ayuso et [SOURCE: Page_297]

761   al. 2014; Blanco-Canqui et al. 2015; Marsac et al. 2019; Meyer et al. 2020). During the first months 762   after cover crop seeding, water profiles are generally the same for fields with cover crops and fields with 763   bare soil because of heavy rainfall (Alonso-Ayuso et al. 2014). However, in the spring, the profiles begin 764   to differ as the cover crop grows, notably if rainfall levels do not compensate for evapotranspiration 765   levels (Alonso-Ayuso et al. 2014; Meyer et al. 2020). The factor with the greatest impact is termination 766   date (Krueger et al. 2011; Alonso-Ayuso et al. 2014; Meyer 2020), followed by crop species, and amount 767   of precipitation (Meyer 2020). Thus, the next crop is likely to face water stress if termination takes place 768   later; if the cover crop produces large quantities of biomass; if climatic conditions are dry; and if water 769   storage capacity is low. Apart from this latter situation, water stress appears to be minimal in the 770   temperate zone, even if termination occurs at a later date, because the soil (particularly the first 771   centimeters) has time to recharge before the next crop is established (Szerencsits 2014; Blanco-Canqui 772   et al. 2015; Marsac et al. 2019; Meyer 2020). These findings suggest there is a risk of water stress for 773   the subsequent crop when cultivating energy cover crops under specific circumstances (i.e., late 774   destruction and high levels of biomass production), an issue that should be studied further. Mean 775   quantities of digestate (30 m^3/ha) contain less than a millimeter of water, which does not at all 776   compensate for water depletion by cover crops. With regards to summer energy cover crops, it is 777   theoretically possible for them to reduce soil temperatures, thus reducing evaporation and leading to 778   greater water reserves than what is seen on bare soil (Blanco-Canqui et al. 2015). While such a result 779   was observed for a multiservice cover crop at one site during a dry year (Blanco-Canqui et al. 2015), it 780   was not observed for energy cover crops at an experimental site in southwestern France (Marsac et al. 781   2019). More studies are needed on this topic. [SOURCE: Page_298]

782       9. The impact of energy cover crops and their digestate on soil physical properties [SOURCE: Page_298]

783   Because they provide cover during periods when the soil would usually be left bare, cover crops reduce 784   wind and water erosion. They are particularly effective at protecting sensitive soils, such as sandy soils 785   (Snapp et al. 2005). Using a meta-analysis, Daryanto et al. (2018) found that, on average, cover crops 786   reduce the amount of soil lost by 75%, compared to situations in which the soil is left bare over the 787   winter. In their study, Du et al. (2022) even found an average reduction of 90% at different points of the 788   globe. The determinant factors were the degree of cover and cover duration (Snapp et al. 2005; Blanco- 789   Canqui et al. 2015). By reducing erosion, cover crops also reduce the loss of dissolved nutrients (e.g., 790   phosphorus and nitrate) via runoff (Blanco-Canqui et al. 2015). In addition to directly protecting the soil 791   from the disturbance caused by rain and wind, cover crops improve soil structural stability (Blanco- 792   Canqui et al. 2015; Daryanto et al. 2018). Cover crops rapidly increase the stability of aggregates (< 3 793   years) by protecting them against the impacts of raindrops; by providing root-mediated carbon inputs; 794   and by boosting microbial activity (Blanco-Canqui et al. 2015). Increasing aggregate stability 795   subsequently increases water retention, carbon storage, macroporosity, and root growth; it decreases the 796   soil’s susceptibility to compaction (Blanco-Canqui et al. 2015). 797   Few studies have looked at the impact of digestate use on the physical properties of soils (Möller 2015). 798   Alburquerque et al. (2012) performed a two-year experiment but found no effect of digestate use on 799   structural stability when compared to other treatments (i.e., no amendment, mineral fertilizer, or cattle 800   manure). Some studies cited in Möller (2015) found a positive effect of digestate use on bulk density, 801   hydraulic conductivity, water retention capacity, and aggregate stability, compared to what was seen for 802   unamended soil. Béghin-Tanneau (2020) also observed an increase in aggregate stability following 803   digestate application over periods of 12 to 265 days. However, the digestate had a significantly weaker 804   effect than its substrate of origin (corn). Similarly, Sarker et al. (2018) found that while digestate use 805   increased aggregate stability, the effect was less pronounced than that seen for alfalfa residues. These 806   results were attributed to a correlation between the decomposability of the organic residues and both 807   soil microbial activity and aggregate stability. [SOURCE: Page_299]

808   Consequently, introducing energy cover crops into crop cycles and utilizing the resulting digestate as 809   fertilizer should help reduce erosion and promote aggregate stability. As these services are furnished 810   during the growing period, they will be unaffected by the fact that energy cover crops are harvested 811   rather than being left in place. On the contrary, service quality should be better than that provided by 812   conventional multiservice cover crops because their magnitude is positively correlated with biomass. 813   That said, energy cover crops have one drawback compared to multiservice cover crops: when three 814   crops are cultivated in two years instead of two, field traffic climbs, increasing the risk of soil 815   compaction (Peters et al. 2016; Quennesson and Decaux 2020). Ensiling the energy cover crops and 816   applying the digestate (Duttmann et al. 2014; Lantz and Börjesson 2014) requires the use of heavier 817   machinery, sometimes under sensitive conditions during the early spring or fall. The risk of soil 818   compaction is particularly high on clay soils and can lead to yield losses (Lantz and Börjesson 2014). 819   However, this risk can be reduced by using tank-free spreading systems (Lantz and Börjesson 2014) or 820   controlled traffic farming systems for silage operations (i.e., the equipment always follows the same 821   path) (Duttmann et al. 2014). Moreover, commonly used energy cover crop species are rarely taproot 822   species, which are able to loosen the soil (Chen and Weil 2010; Blanco-Canqui et al. 2015). [SOURCE: Page_299]

823       10. Impacts on cropping systems and farms [SOURCE: Page_299]

824               a. Food/feed production [SOURCE: Page_299]

825   In the previous sections, we noted that energy cover crops can reduce the yield of subsequent crops 826   because of preemptive competition for water and nitrogen and because of increased soil compaction 827   risks. However, the greatest potential deleterious effect of energy cover crops on subsequent crops is 828   associated with the delay in seeding and the use of early varieties (Szerencsits 2014; Marsac et al. 2019). 829   Szerencsits (2014) observed that the yield of spring crops declined by an average of 10% if seeding was 830   delayed by more than 7 days, and Marsac et al. (2019) observed a 7% loss in yield if the delay attained 831   10–15 days. When the delay was even longer (one month or more), the next cash crop could not reach [SOURCE: Page_299]

832   maturity before harvest. Thus, the cash crop can no longer feed humans but can be used to feed animals 833   or can undergo anaerobic digestion (Graß et al. 2013; Peters et al. 2016; Quennesson and Decaux 2020). 834   In such systems, the objective is to optimize the production of both crops in tandem, and both crops are 835   harvested before maturity. In such cases, there is no longer a clear distinction between the cash crop and 836   the cover crop. These systems do not align with the intended purpose of energy cover crops, which is to 837   produce biomass for energy purposes without replacing food crops. The widespread use of such systems 838   in areas where food crops are grown could end up reducing overall food production (Kemp and Lyutse 839   2011; WWF France 2020). [SOURCE: Page_300]

840               b. Nitrogen balance at the farm level [SOURCE: Page_300]

841   A survey program in France contacted farmers with anaerobic digesters and obtained data to calculate 842   the nitrogen balance on their farms. Unfortunately, most were livestock farmers, and only a small 843   number (9 out of 46) had introduced energy cover crops to their crop rotations. None of these nine farms 844   increased their mineral fertilizer consumption following the introduction of anaerobic digestion and 845   energy cover crops. Four of them even reduced their mineral nitrogen fertilizer purchases (ADEME and 846   Solagro 2018). However, this survey does not allow us to isolate the impact of energy cover crops. 847   Anaerobic digestion is often accompanied by other changes in farm practices and, above all, by 848   exchanges of materials with neighboring farms, industries and collectivities. In addition, these farms 849   still have insufficient hindsight on their new production system to observe long-term effects on soil 850   fertility. According to field trials or simulations, introducing a third fertilized crop within a two-year 851   rotation would likely mean an increased need for nitrogen (Heggenstaller et al. 2008; Igos et al. 2016; 852   Berti et al. 2017; Girault et al. 2019). Additional nitrogen would be required to meet the energy cover 853   crop’s needs and, possibly, to compensate the following crop for nitrogen lost between the ensiling of 854   the energy cover crop and the application of the resulting digestate; there could also be preemptive 855   competition for nitrogen. The use of synthetic fertilizers could be reduced by codigesting farm-derived 856   biomass with externally derived biomass or by using legumes alone or in mixture as energy cover crops. [SOURCE: Page_300]

857               c. Life cycle assessment [SOURCE: Page_300]

858   A recently released Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) found that an anaerobic digestion scenario with 50% 859   energy cover crops in the feedstock supply performed better than a non-biogas scenario with 860   multiservice cover crops on indicators of energetic resource depletion, climate change and ozone 861   depletion (Esnouf et al. 2021). This study considered the production of heat energy through the 862   combustion of methane injected into the network, the management of livestock effluents and soil 863   fertilization. The finality of the biogas produced had a strong impact on these indicators. In LCAs 864   studying biogas transformed by cogeneration, the poor valorization of heat completely degrades the 865   environmental balance of the anaerobic digestion (Bacenetti et al. 2016; Hijazi et al. 2016). If we look 866   at the greenhouse gas balance in more detail, the studies agree that double cropping increased i) nitrogen [SOURCE: Page_300]

867   fertilizer use and therefore N2O emissions in the field or CO$_2$ emissions upstream and ii) field operations 868   and thus CO$_2$ emissions from fuel combustion (Igos et al. 2016; Berti et al. 2017; Maier et al. 2017; 869   Esnouf et al. 2021). However, the soil C storage and above all the substitution of fossil gas largely 870   compensated these side-effects in the study of Esnouf et al. (2021) where the anaerobic digestion 871   scenario reduced by 75% the greenhouse gas emissions. The indicators of fine particle emissions, 872   environmental acidification and terrestrial eutrophication that were also measured in this study depend 873   to a very large extent on ammonia emissions during storage and spreading of the effluent and digestate. 874   In this case, adopting anaerobic digestion with good storage and spreading practices improved the 875   performance on these indicators compared to the reference scenario. Conversely, not covering the 876   digestate could increase greenhouse gas emissions by 80% (Bacenetti et al. 2016; Esnouf et al. 2021). 877   Finally, still in the same study, for indicators related to electricity consumption and fertilizer 878   consumption, the performance was worse with anaerobic digestion but the introduction of legumes in 879   energy cover crops and the optimization of digestate spreading equipment could reduce these impacts 880   by 10 to 50%. The use of legumes had already been noted to reduce the greenhouse gas balance related 881   to the reduction of the use of synthetic fertilizers and the reduction of N2O emissions (Stinner 2015). 882   Other LCAs exist in the literature but they rather study energy crops whose impact on land use change 883   strongly influences the performance on the climate change indicator (Bacenetti et al. 2016; Igos et al. 884   2016; Hijazi et al. 2016). Styles et al. (2015) compared different energy production systems, including 885   one in which corn serves as a summer energy cover crop or as a simple energy crop. They found that 886   the greenhouse gas balance of the first system was rather neutral compared to the baseline system. In 887   contrast, anaerobically digesting dedicated crops increased emissions, notably because additional land 888   was needed to compensate for the loss in food production. [SOURCE: Page_301]

889       11. Conclusions [SOURCE: Page_301]

890   This review reveals that the use of energy cover crops and their digestates has several advantages. In 891   addition to allowing the production of renewable energy, the crops can provide several ecosystem 892   services, including improved water quality, climate change mitigation, reduced soil erosion, and 893   increased microbial activity. Thus, to answer the question raised in the introduction, we can still consider 894   them as multiservice cover crops. However, they could also have some disservices, such as reduced 895   groundwater recharge and the need for increased nitrogen inputs. Furthermore, energy cover crops are 896   not always used as intended, leading to competition with food crops. Energy cover crops can compete 897   with food crops for water and nutrients. This competition can be limited if there are sufficient levels of 898   spring precipitation and if fertilizer is used. Additionally, incorporating energy cover crops into rotations 899   induces changes in cropping systems that can lead to certain excesses, where energy cover crop 900   production is favored to the detriment of food crop production. Cropping systems should be designed 901   so as to maximize the non-energy-related services provided by energy cover crops. Alternatively, trade- 902   offs should be identified, such that energy cover crops can be treated more as multiservice cover crops [SOURCE: Page_301]

903   than as cash crops. In this way, farmers would view energy cover crops not only as a new income source, 904   but also as a way to improve their fields over the long term (e.g., via increased soil organic matter, 905   improved soil structural stability, decreased pest pressure). Some research is still needed to expect 906   widespread adoption of energy cover crops by farmers. We can suggest a few leads. At the varietal 907   selection level, improvements are possible to adapt forage species to double cropping. In terms of 908   technical management, the problem of summer cover crops establishment need a solution; seeding under 909   cover could be an opportunity to explore. Finally, at the academic level, we have a great deal of 910   knowledge about cover crops and digestates that allows us to speculate on the impacts of energy cover 911   crops. They remained to be confronted with the field in a wide variety of situations. [SOURCE: Page_302]

Insertion of energy cover crops in cropping systems in France: multi-scale assessment of production potential and water - nitrogen - carbon impacts. Author: Camille Launay Supervision: Sabine Houot (UMR EcoSys), Julie Constantin (UMR AGIR), Vincent Jean-Baptiste (GRDF) Place and date of defense: Toulouse on July 3, 2023 Agricultural anaerobic digestion (AD), a biogas production process, is currently expanding rapidly in Europe thanks to the support of public policies. Cover crops, i.e. crops grown between two main crops, could provide a considerable amount of biomass for anaerobic digestion, especially on farms without livestock. Until now, cover crops were neither fertilized nor harvested, and were sometimes mandatory in order to limit groundwater contamination because they capture nitrate (catch crops, CCs). They can also provide other ecosystem services (multi-services cover crops, MSCCs). With the development of anaerobic digestion, the management of cover crops is changing to produce more biomass. They are fertilized, potentially with AD digestate, and harvested before maturity. They are then referred to as energy cover crops (ECCs). There are two questions concerning ECCs: (i) on the amount of energy that ECCs could produce on a national scale, a question addressed via the evaluation of potential biomass production on a French scale, (ii) on the impacts associated with their intensification and the return of digestates to the soil in comparison with MSCCs and CCs. We studied the impacts studied concerning main crop production, greenhouse gas emissions, nitrate leaching, ammonia volatilization, changes in soil organic matter stocks, and water consumption. To this end, we set up an approach combining field experimentation and modeling, and then deployed a modeling chain on a territorial scale over the long-term and subsequently throughout France. The STICS model was used to simulate crop production and the impact of cropping systems on environmental variables. It was coupled to the ALFAM2 model for ammonia volatilization after organic fertilizer application and to the SYS-Metha model for the AD process of ECCs. We found that ECCs could be a significant source of energy in France. Depending on the assumptions made about the level of deployment of ECCs, the harvesting threshold and the cutting height, the resource could be multiplied by seven (from 17 to 115 TWh) and significantly exceed previous estimates (from 6 to 55 TWh). Regarding environmental impacts, ECCs are indeed a lever for climate change mitigation despite their fertilization and the associated increase in N2O emissions. In addition to substituting fossil gas with biomethane, they store more C in soils than MSCCs due to their larger biomass. They also reduce nitrate pollution but to a lesser extent than CCs because the species chosen are less efficient. It is very likely that ECCs will reduce food production by reducing the yield of the spring crops that follow them. We observed both nitrogen stress that could be compensated for by increased fertilization and water stress compensated for by increased irrigation. MSCCs can also have a negative impact on the yield of the following crop, but their flexible management offers several levers of avoidance (e.g. choice of species, destruction date). Increased fertilization in crop sequences integrating ECCs decreases the mitigation of fossil fuel dependence and increases ammonia volatilization and thus air pollution. Finally, both MSCCs and ECCs increase water consumption, which decreases potential groundwater recharge and water availability for the next crop. The species of cover crop used is the first factor of variation, followed by the quantity of biomass produced. [SOURCE: Page_320]
